column2: Real and typical foundation failure cases: work out from the clues what happened and what would have prevented it. With a crack-reading game.

The ground tipped a silo to 27° in a single day. A tower block fell onto its side in one piece. The riverbed ran out from under a bridge pier. You are the expert: from the clues you have to work out what happened and what would have prevented it. Every case belongs to a lecture of the course. The fewer clues you need to solve it, the more points you get.
Choose a case. The first clue is free; open the others only if you need them.
The cracks in a wall reveal how the foundation beneath it has moved. Look at the façade and decide which settlement shape caused it.
BME Department of Engineering Geology and Geotechnics · Foundation Engineering · The figures are schematic. The typical cases are invented, but they occur regularly in Hungarian practice.
Tilted grain elevator with clay bulging out of the ground
Tower block lying on its side, with a spoil heap and an excavation beside it
Tilted tower on soft clay layers, with a high water table
Single-storey house with cracked walls on dried-out clay, a tree nearby
House settled at one corner on loess, with a leaking pipe next to the corner
Unheated garage on a shallow foundation, ice lenses in the ground
Collapsed bridge span and a toppled pier in the flooded river
Collapsed strutted excavation in soft clay

A huge reinforced concrete grain elevator on a single 23.5 × 59.5 m raft. On its first filling, at 87.5 % of capacity, it settled 30 cm in an hour, and within a day it had tilted to about 27°.
Beneath the raft lies thick lake clay. The deeper layers are softer: their undrained shear strength is about 30 kPa.
The silo was hardly damaged; it rotated as a whole, like a rigid body. Next to the side that went down, the ground heaved up.
The bearing resistance calculated with the undrained shear strength came out at about 307 kPa. The contact pressure actually acting at failure was about 297 kPa.
Bearing failure: the load reached the bearing resistance of the clay, and a slip surface formed beneath the raft
Consolidation settlement that built up over years
The reinforced concrete structure broke and tipped over

Rotation to one side within a day, heaving ground, an intact structure: this is the fingerprint of bearing failure. Consolidation takes months or years, and a structural failure would have torn the silo apart.
Checking the bearing resistance with the undrained shear strength, or carrying the load down to the deeper bearing stratum
Stronger concrete in the silo walls
A taller silo with a smaller footprint

The stiffness of the raft and the strength of the concrete do not increase the bearing resistance of the ground. On soft clay under rapid loading, the undrained bearing resistance governs, and it has to be checked.
In 1914 the silo was tilted back: 14 piers were taken down to rock beneath the raised side, and the structure was brought back to vertical by about 3.7 m. It still works as a grain store today.
The Transcona elevator became one of the most important confirmations of soil mechanics: the failure load back-calculated with the undrained shear strength hardly differed from the actual one.
A 13-storey residential building, not yet handed over, fell onto its side in one piece at dawn. Its structure stayed almost intact.
Prestressed concrete pipe piles, 33 m long and 40 cm in diameter. Beneath the building the piles broke near their heads.

On the south side of the building, about 7 m away, a 4.6 m deep excavation was being dug for an underground garage. The excavated soil was piled up on the north side, barely 1 m from the building, to a height of about 10 m.
It had rained for days beforehand. The plot lies on the bank of a creek, and the upper layers are soft, saturated clays. The building fell towards the excavation, to the south.
The piles were too short, and the building slowly sank under its own weight
The soft ground under the spoil heap slipped and was squeezed sideways under the building: the piles were loaded laterally, and the building tipped towards the excavation
The building broke in two because of poor-quality concrete

The building rotated as a whole towards the excavation, and the piles broke at their heads. This was not slow settlement: the 10 m high spoil heap caused a general bearing failure in the soaked, soft clay, and the slipping soil was pushed under the building towards the excavation.
What is the most important lesson?
A tower block may only be placed on a shallow foundation
Concrete must not be placed in the rain
No large spoil heaps next to buildings and excavations – and piles are also loaded by lateral ground movement
A pile carries vertical load well, but soil moving past it bends it sideways. On soft ground a spoil heap behaves like a slope: its stability should also have been verified.

According to the investigation, the excavated soil was piled up next to the building and the pit was dug on the other side. Later analyses found that after the rain an undrained bearing failure developed under the spoil heap, and the pressure of the slipping soil tipped the building over. One worker died.
A “messy” construction site is a geotechnical issue too: the spoil heap is a load, the excavation is unloading, and together they add up in the worst possible place.
spoil heap next to the building
deep pit on the far side

Construction of the bell tower began in 1173, and the tilt appeared during construction. With two long pauses the work lasted nearly 200 years, and the builders tried to compensate by building the later storeys at an angle.
Beneath the tower lie soft, compressible layers of clay and silt, with groundwater 1–2 m below the surface. Under the south side the ground is slightly more compressible.
A relatively shallow, ring-shaped foundation beneath a tall, slender tower with a mass of about 14 500 t.
The tilt accelerated in the 20th century. In 1993 the foundation was inclined at 5.4°, and the top cornice overhung by 4.1 m.
A bearing failure that happened in a single day
The masonry crushed under the load
Uneven compression of the soft clay: the south side settled slightly more, and the tilt itself increased the load on that side

This is a slow process over centuries: differential settlement tilted the tower, and the centre of gravity of the leaning tower moved towards the lower side, putting even more load on the ground there. A tall, slender structure is especially sensitive to this.
How was it stabilised between 1999 and 2001?
Soil was extracted from under the north side through inclined boreholes, so that this side would settle slightly
The south side was raised by grouting
The whole tower was placed on piles
The upper storeys were dismantled and rebuilt
Controlled settlement of the opposite side is the least intrusive intervention: the tower received no new load, and the weaker south side was not disturbed.
Soil was extracted from dozens of inclined boreholes under the north side, reducing the tilt by about 0.5°. The tower was closed in 1990 and reopened in 2001 after the work.
With settlement it is not just the amount that matters: differential settlement and how easily the structure tips decide together whether there will be trouble.
Great Hungarian Plain · typical Hungarian case
A single-storey family house on 0.8 m deep strip footings, on yellow, high-plasticity clay. After a summer of drought, diagonal cracks appeared at the corners and the doors stick.
A row of 15-year-old poplars stands 4 m from the corner of the house.
In autumn, after the rains, the cracks partly closed, and the following summer they opened again.
The corners settled the most, the middle of the long walls the least. The difference is 2–3 cm.
The clay shrank under the edges of the house as it dried out in summer, especially towards the trees, and it swells again in the wet season

Expansive clay changes its volume together with its water content. The 0.8 m deep foundation lies within the drying zone, and the tree roots dry the ground out even deeper. Recurring seasonal movement is typical of this soil.
Grouting the ground around the house
Plastering over the cracks and repainting
Taking the foundation below the desiccation zone, for example by mass concrete underpinning or micropiles, and keeping trees away from the house
Planting more trees around the house
The movement is caused by the drying zone. As long as the foundation stays within it, the cracks come back every dry summer. Grouting and plastering do not remove the cause.

This kind of damage appears on a large scale in drought years in the clay areas of the Great Plain. The solution is always to get the foundation out of the zone where the water content changes with the seasons.
On expansive clay the frost line is not deep enough: the foundation level must be below the desiccation zone, and the water uptake of trees must also be taken into account.
A corner that sank in a week
Transdanubian loess plateau · typical Hungarian case
A single-storey house, standing for twenty years on 1.0 m deep strip footings on loess. Within a week one corner of the house settled 8 cm, and the wall cracked diagonally.
Before the settlement, the water pipe in the garden burst, and water leaked next to the corner for days.
Dry loess stands even in vertical faces. Crumbled by hand it is loose and porous, and riddled with tiny vertical channels.
The sample was soaked under load: it compressed suddenly and by a large amount.
The loess swelled and lifted the rest of the house
The water soaking in dissolved the bonds holding the grains together, and the loess collapsed beneath the corner
Collapsible loess is strong when dry, but its loose skeleton collapses when it is soaked. Sudden settlement concentrated around the water source points to this, and the laboratory test confirms it.
Eliminating the water source, draining rainwater away and strengthening the corner by mass concrete underpinning or micropiles
Tying the walls together with steel straps; there is no need to deal with the ground
Waiting until the loess swells back by itself
First the path of the water has to be cut off, because the collapse can continue until then. After that, the foundation has to be taken below the soaked, collapsed zone.
In loess areas, a burst pipe, poor rainwater drainage or overwatering the garden often causes sudden damage, decades later, to a house that had been fine until then.
On loess, water is the greatest enemy: drainage and watertight paving are part of the foundation.
An unheated, lightweight garden garage on 40 cm deep strip footings in silty clay. At the end of January the up-and-over door jammed, and a crack opened in the corner.
The door started working again by itself, and the crack partly closed.
The drain next to the garage got blocked in winter, and the water ran down beside the wall.
Horizontal ice lenses were found in the ground, 10–30 cm deep.
Summer drying of the swelling clay
Frost heave: ice lenses grew in the moist, silty soil above the frost line and lifted the foundation
It moved in winter and recovered in spring: this is frost. Silty soil draws water up into the frozen zone, where it freezes into ice lenses and lifts whatever is above it.
What would the correct foundation have been?
A shallower foundation, so that less soil freezes beneath it
A lighter roof on the garage
Foundation level below the frost line – in Budapest at least 0.8 m – and draining the water away from the wall
Ice lenses cannot lift a foundation placed below the frost line. Frost lifts a light building even more easily, so weight is no protection.
Unheated outbuildings, fence footings and garden retaining walls are the most common victims: under a heated house the ground freezes less deeply, but beside them it freezes to the full depth.
The frost line applies to every foundation, and to light buildings in particular. Silt is the most frost-susceptible soil.
A steel bridge over the Douro, built in 1886. On the evening of 4 March 2001 the fourth pier collapsed, and a bus and three cars fell into the river.
The winter brought months of flooding: for three months the discharge was above 2000 m³/s.
From the 1970s, large quantities of sand were extracted from the river. Next to the pier, the riverbed deepened by a total of about 13 m between 1913 and 1989.
Damage to the pier foundation had already been visible earlier.
Scour: the flood carried away the sediment around the pier, and in a riverbed already deepened by sand extraction the ground ran out from under the pier
Over decades the deepening riverbed took away the embedment of the pier foundation, and the flood washed out the rest. The pier failed from its foundation, not from the superstructure.
Taking the pier foundations below the expected scour depth, protecting the riverbed with rock armour and surveying the riverbed regularly
Rebuilding the bridge from lighter materials
Extracting more sand to deepen the riverbed
Scour is countered by foundation depth and by protecting the riverbed. Changes in the riverbed have to be monitored, because sand extraction and floods alter it year by year.
59 people died in the disaster. The minister of transport resigned the next day. The new bridge, 7 m further up the river, was opened in 2002.
The movement of water is a load on foundations: a foundation standing in a riverbed has to be designed against scour just as it is for vertical load.
Construction of a metro station and tunnel: a strutted excavation about 30 m deep in soft marine clay, next to a busy main road.
The walls of the excavation were supported by steel struts and walings. The collapse started with the failure of a waling–strut connection and then spread like a chain reaction.
Weeks earlier, the instruments measuring the wall movements had shown displacements larger than allowed – and the alarm level was raised.
The undrained behaviour of the soft clay was modelled in a way that gave a higher shear strength than the real one.
Hydraulic failure at the base of the excavation
An undersized connection in the strutting failed: the wrongly calculated, too-low forces and the ignored measurements together led to the chain-reaction collapse
The load of the traffic on the surface

The weak point was the waling–strut connection, and because of the over-optimistic soil model the forces calculated for the wall and the struts were lower than the real ones. The measurements signalled the trouble, but the limit was raised instead of stopping the work.
The alarm level has to be raised if the measured value exceeds it
Fewer instruments are needed, so that they do not disturb the work
A deeper excavation has to be dug
Monitoring is part of the design: if the measured movement exceeds the limit, you have to stop and redesign
The observational method only protects you if decisions are based on the measured data. The safety of an excavation is the joint responsibility of design, construction and monitoring.
Four people died. The committee of inquiry found human and organisational errors. The route of the metro line was changed, and the station was built elsewhere.
In a deep excavation, monitoring is not paperwork: wall movement is the first sign, and it has to be taken seriously.

Diagonal cracks rise towards the larger settlement – here up to the right. The right-hand part of the wall moved down relative to the left-hand part.
Diagonal cracks rise towards the larger settlement – here up to the left. The left-hand part of the wall settled more.
In the middle the crack is wider at the bottom: the bottom fibre of the wall is in tension, like that of a sagging beam. The diagonal cracks rise towards the middle.

In the middle the crack is wider at the top: the top fibre of the wall is in tension. The diagonal cracks rise towards the corners. Typical of houses on shrinking clay, where the ground dries out under the corners.
Not this one. Look at which way the diagonal cracks rise, and where the middle crack is wider.

Rule of thumb: a diagonal crack rises towards the larger settlement; a vertical crack is wider where the wall is in tension – at the bottom for a sagging shape, at the top for a hogging one.
